newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: FOCUS-Zimbabwe central bank cuts key rate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Zimbabwe central bank cuts key rate.

text.p: Zimbabwe's central Reserve Bank said on Wednesday it had lowered its key rediscount rate to 27 percent from 27.5 percent, citing a decline in annual inflation.
It said it expected year-on-year consumer inflation -- which ticked up to 20.6 percent in September from a three-year-low of 17.7 percent in August -- to end 1996 at just above 20 percent.
"In view of this outlook, coupled with the downward trend experienced so far, the bank has lowered the rediscount rate from 27.5 percent to 27 percent," it said in a statement.
This is the second time in two months that the bank has adjusted the benchmark rate at which it lends to financial institutions.
In August, it sliced off two percentage points from the rate, bringing it to 27.5 percent, its first cut since November 1994 when it lowered it to 29.5 percent from 30 percent.
On Wednesday, the Reserve Bank said it would reduce its rediscount rate further if consumer inflation maintained its downward trend.
"Evidence of a continued deceleration of inflation will, of course, see the bank further reduce the rediscount rate, in that way supporting recovery of the productive sectors," it said.

It said the upward move in year-on-year consumer price inflation in September was anticipated and was a temporary reversal of its downward trend largely due to lagged effects of recent private and public sector wage settlements, fuel price hikes and periodic adjustments of administered prices.

"The impact of the October round of fuel price increases, coupled with that of the 20 percent civil service wage adjustment, will have a bearing on price developments to the end of the year," it said.

"The bank, therefore, still anticipates inflation to the end of 1996 to be just above 20 percent," it added. This was a slight revision upwards of earlier projections by the bank which pegged annual inflation at 20 percent by December from a peak of 28 percent at the beginning of the year.

The lower rediscount rate has boosted hopes in the private sector that the southern African country was finally breaking out of its cycle of punitive interest rates which industrialists have blamed for driving scores of firms into bankruptcy over the past five years.

In August, commercial banks pre-empted the central bank by cutting their minimum lending rates to 30 percent from around 32 percent, citing prospects of lower inflation and a fall in money market rates.
Economic and money market analysts as well as the country's industrialists have been expecting further lending rate cuts following the Reserve Bank rediscount rate adjustment.
One of the country's biggest commercial banks, Standard Chartered Zimbabwe, on Monday reduced its minimum lending rate a further 1.5 percentage points to 28.5 percent.
